analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to use manipulative or deceptive tricks in wholesale electricity markets.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron scandal, in which traders used schemes to drive up wholesale electricity prices, Senator Maria Cantwell proposed writing an explicit ban on market manipulation into the Federal Power Act. The bill would make it unlawful to use any manipulative or deceptive device in buying or selling wholesale electricity or transmission service, and would treat any rates that resulted from manipulation as unreasonable — meaning regulators could reject or refund them. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy electricity. Ratepayers bear the cost of manipulation schemes that inflate wholesale power prices, because those inflated costs flow into utility rates. The bill would give federal regulators explicit authority to police manipulative trading and to unwind rates that resulted from it.

how_it_helps.text: Declares unlawful the use of any manipulative or deceptive device or contrivance in the purchase or sale of electric energy or transmission services under FERC jurisdiction, when done contrary to FERC regulations.
Amends the Federal Power Act so that rates resulting from a manipulative or deceptive device are treated as not just and reasonable, allowing regulators to reject or refund them.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers and energy trading firms, which could no longer profit from manipulative or deceptive trading schemes and could be forced to give back rates earned through them. Honest market participants would face compliance and enforcement costs.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition only covers devices used in contravention of regulations FERC may promulgate, so ratepayers get no protection until and unless the agency writes and enforces anti-manipulation rules.

The ban covers any 'manipulative or deceptive device' across wholesale power and transmission markets; a good-faith objection is that broad, agency-defined manipulation rules could sweep in legitimate hedging and trading strategies, and disputes over them could raise costs for power sellers that flow into rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ratepayers is real: explicit anti-manipulation authority and the ability to void rates earned through manipulation directly target the practices behind the Enron-era price spikes. The cost falls on firms that were manipulating markets, plus modest compliance costs for others. The main design weakness is that the bill's force depends on FERC choosing to write and enforce the rules. On balance it is a plainly consumer-protective bill whose costs fall on the industry whose conduct it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the ENRON Act on January 24, 2005, joined by Senators Bingaman, Feinstein, Murray, and Feingold as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; the sponsor gave introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.
The bill received six cosponsors: five Democrats and one Independent.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firms selling into wholesale electricity markets were better off because the bill died: no federal anti-manipulation standard or rate-refund mechanism was added to the Federal Power Act, and the practices the bill targeted remained subject only to whatever rules regulators already had. Ratepayers received no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers and energy traders

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 24, 2005 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pete Domenici
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in the committee controlled by the Republican majority without a vote that would have shown the full chamber's split.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers and energy trading firms
industries.note: The bill would have made manipulative and deceptive trading in wholesale power markets unlawful and voided the rates that resulted from it, threatening exactly the tactics that produced windfall profits during the Enron-era price spikes. Those firms' gain from blocking the bill came at ratepayers' expense.

industries.industry: FERC-regulated electric utilities and power sellers
industries.note: All FERC-jurisdictional wholesale sellers, including conventional utilities, would face new anti-manipulation rules and compliance costs, but honest firms also benefit from markets where manipulation is policed because it keeps prices and transmission access trustworthy.
